stem:
A GP sees a 4-week-old term boy who is still jaundiced. He is breastfed, feeding well and has gained 600 g above his birth weight. His mother says his stools have become pale over the past week and his urine now leaves a yellow stain on the nappy. Examination is otherwise normal, with no hepatosplenomegaly.

Which blood test should the GP request today?

options.label: A
options.text: Total serum bilirubin, repeated in one week
options.explanation: A total level cannot distinguish conjugated from unconjugated bilirubin, and a week of waiting can matter in biliary atresia.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct antiglobulin test and reticulocyte count
options.explanation: These assess haemolysis, which causes unconjugated jaundice and does not explain pale stools or dark urine.

options.label: C
options.text: Thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4)
options.explanation: Hypothyroidism can prolong unconjugated jaundice, but it does not explain pale stools and does not identify the bilirubin fraction.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct. Fractionation identifies conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Prolonged jaundice with pale stools and dark urine needs this today and urgent paediatric assessment for cholestasis, including biliary atresia.

options.label: E
options.text: G6PD enzyme assay and a blood film
options.explanation: This tests a cause of haemolysis and does not assess the cholestatic pattern.

context: A thriving appearance does not make pale stools benign. Fractionated bilirubin is essential when prolonged jaundice accompanies pale stools or dark urine.
